THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS COOK, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $33010.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. The register states this purchaser's residence as COOK, so the sale is contemporary evidence that a man of this name lived in Cook County on the date of sale. It is not evidence that he lived in the town. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: PEARSONS HIRAM matches Hiram Pearsons: the forename names Hiram Pearsons of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Charles Spicer
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Spicer, Charles' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 6 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

persons.name: Mitchel Ouillemett
persons.note: CARDED FROM THE BORDERLINE ROSTER'S R6 (T-1376, stage `underdocumented`). Enrolled at Chicago in 1832 in the company the Black Hawk War roll heads INDIAN, with no 1835 corroboration and no card. The licence is R3's — the same roll, the same year, the same page — and the twenty men of Kercheval's company the town already carries were re-admitted under it. The roll prints him as `OUILLEMETT, MITCHEL`, company `INDIAN`, enrolled at `CHICAGO`. The research READ this name and WITHHELD it, and that refusal is not overturned: this record is a reconstruction of what the town looks like if the name is admitted at the limit of its own evidence, and it says so on its face. The reading, the source and the refusal stand at `civic:data/research/civic/records/blackhawk_war_1832_chicago.json#records/blackhawk_1832_081#0` in data/reconstruction/1835_borderline_roster.json. REVIEW REQUIRED: this card is a record of a Native person at Chicago in the three years of the removal, and AGENTS.md's standing constraint holds it for review by Native scholars or community organisations before any scene carrying it may be marked released. No figure is drawn (L1).

persons.name: John Wright
persons.note: ONE OF THE TWELVE WHO VOTED FOR INCORPORATION on 5 August 1833 (Andreas prints the poll: 'John W. Wright'), one of the twenty-eight electors five days later, a candidate who took two votes, and one of the nine village citizens founding the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833 and one of its three first elders. Charles Butler met him on his first morning in Chicago in August 1833, at the funeral of a child. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds, and an advertisement in it is a peculiarly good witness: the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him. It is also NINETEEN MONTHS before the scene date, in the town's fastest-changing period, so it is strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835.

persons.name: John S. Wright
persons.note: A MINOR IN 1833 AND A FOUNDING MEMBER OF THE FIRST PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN JUNE OF THAT YEAR - his name is in the list of nine village citizens alongside his father's. He would have been about twenty in 1835. THE RELATIONSHIP IS THIS RECORD'S READING: Andreas lists the two Wrights separately and never says they are father and son, and 'John Wright, came in 1832, a merchant' and 'John S. Wright, then a minor ... came in 1832' arriving in the same year with the same surname and joining the same church on the same day is a strong reading and not a statement.

residents.research_note: A FATHER-AND-SON HOUSEHOLD ASSEMBLED FROM TWO SEPARATE ROSTER ENTRIES, and one of only three multi-generation households in this parcel. THE ADVERTISEMENT IS WORTH MORE THAN THE PEOPLE HERE: 'Two Buildings to Let' until 1 June 1834 documents a rental market in a town of perhaps a thousand people, and this project holds a trap about that same advertisement - it carries an engraving of a three-storey building which is a jobbing printer's stock cut and NOT a picture of anything in Chicago.
